fatal_errors: The hypothesis assumes an initially single-phase FCC alloy, whereas the target material is the as-cast dual-phase FCC+B2 AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEA.
It replaces the decisive intermediate-temperature aging intervention with low-temperature/high-strain-rate mechanical testing.

It assigns failure to grain-boundary short-range ordering and reduced cohesion rather than L12 ordering within FCC domains, elevated APBE and modulus, planar slip, and stress concentration at jagged FCC/B2 phase-boundary tips.
It does not predict the specific non-monotonic ductile-brittle-ductile aging response, including minimum ductility near 600°C and recovery near 750°C.
The cited evidence does not establish dynamic grain-boundary short-range ordering as the proposed cause of embrittlement.
explanation: The response addresses the broad question of embrittlement without coarse precipitation and offers an internally falsifiable alternative, but it does not reconstruct the target material, intervention, temperature window, structural mediator, or fracture mechanism. Its only meaningful overlap is the general role of chemical ordering and an expectation of improved ductility at higher temperature. The proposed measurements could test its own grain-boundary-cohesion hypothesis, yet they omit the decisive comparison among as-cast, approximately 600°C-aged, and approximately 750°C-aged states and do not seek dislocation pile-ups or crack initiation at jagged FCC/B2 phase-boundary tips. E1 supports conventional segregation and precipitation mechanisms, while E2 discusses possible boundary decohesion or nanoclustering; neither directly supports stress-induced short-range-order formation at grain boundaries. Thus the alternative is testable but presently insufficiently evidenced and scientifically mismatched to the hidden result.
